'''Nir Ben-Tal''' (Hebrew: ניר בן-טל) is an Israeli [[computational biologist]] and professor in the School of Neurobiology, Biochemistry and Biophysics of the George S. Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, [[Tel Aviv University]]. He holds the [[Abraham E. Kazan]] Chair of [[Structural Biology]], Tel Aviv University. His research focuses on [[Structural biology|computational structural biology]], [[structural bioinformatics]], [[protein evolution]], and the relationships among [[protein sequence]], [[structure]], dynamics, and function.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title='How life began merits a preceding discussion of what life actually is' |url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/opinions/090822/book-from-molecules-to-life |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=www.asbmb.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nepomnyachiy |first1=Sergey |last2=Ben-Tal |first2=Nir |last3=Kolodny |first3=Rachel |date=2017-10-31 |title=Complex evolutionary footprints revealed in an analysis of reused protein segments of diverse lengths |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=114 |issue=44 |pages=11703–11708 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1707642114 |doi-access=free |pmc=5676897 |pmid=29078314 |bibcode=2017PNAS..11411703N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Uniting sequence and structure to map the protein universe |url=https://www.isct.ac.jp/en/news/710omgmrx88a |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=Science Tokyo |language=en}}</ref>

== Education and academic career ==
Ben-Tal studied biology, chemistry, and physics at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], receiving his bachelor's degree in 1988.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Prof. Nir Ben-Tal {{!}} The George S. Wise Faculty of Life Sciences |url=https://en-lifesci.tau.ac.il/profile/bental |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=en-lifesci.tau.ac.il}}</ref> He subsequently earned a D.Sc. in chemistry from the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]] in 1993, under the supervision of Professor Nimrod Moiseyev. He completed postdoctoral training with Professor [[Barry H. Honig|Barry Honig]] in biophysical chemistry and computational biophysics at [[Columbia University|Columbia University in New York]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Prof. Nir Ben-Tal |url=https://english.tau.ac.il/profile/bental |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=Tel Aviv University |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1997, Ben-Tal joined the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at [[Tel Aviv University]]. He became a full professor in 2007. He is a member of the university's School of Neurobiology, Biochemistry and Biophysics and also serves as head of the Bioinformatics Master program within the Faculty of Life Sciences.<ref name=":2" />

In 2018, Ben-Tal was awarded the Abraham E. Kazan Chair of Structural Biology at [[Tel Aviv University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=August 2018: Ben-Tal awarded the Kazan Chair |url=https://en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il/nir_ben_tal_chair_award |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research ==
Ben-Tal's research is in [[Structural biology|computational structural biology]], with an emphasis on developing computational methods to study protein structure, function, motion, and evolution.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elofsson |first1=Arne |last2=Ben-Tal |first2=Nir |date=2026-07-08 |title=What will be the future of computational biology for macromolecules in the era of AI? |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |language=en |publisher=Public Library of Science |volume=22 |issue=7 |article-number=e1014467 |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014467  |doi-access=free|issn=1553-7358 |pmc=13345252 |pmid=42418429 |bibcode=2026PLSCB..2214467E }}</ref> His laboratory investigates molecular systems for which computational approaches can provide information that is difficult to obtain experimentally.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |title=The Ben-Tal Lab of Computational Structural Biology - Ramot |url=https://ramot.org/services/the-ben-tal-lab-of-computational-structural-biology/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260515080406/https://ramot.org/services/the-ben-tal-lab-of-computational-structural-biology/ |archive-date=2026-05-15 |access-date=2026-09-24 |work=Ramot |language=en-US}}</ref>

His research has included computational studies of membrane [[Protein|proteins]] and transporters, including the human copper transporter 1<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schushan |first1=Maya |last2=Barkan |first2=Yariv |last3=Haliloglu |first3=Turkan |last4=Ben-Tal |first4=Nir |date=2010-06-15 |title=C(alpha)-trace model of the transmembrane domain of human copper transporter 1, motion and functional implications |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=107 |issue=24 |pages=10908–10913 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0914717107 |doi-access=free |issn=1091-6490 |pmc=2890728 |pmid=20534491}}</ref>, the [[Wilson disease protein|ATP7B]] copper-transporting [[ATPase]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schushan |first1=Maya |last2=Bhattacharjee |first2=Ashima |last3=Ben-Tal |first3=Nir |last4=Lutsenko |first4=Svetlana |date=2012 |title=A structural model of the copper ATPase ATP7B to facilitate analysis of Wilson disease-causing mutations and studies of the transport mechanism |journal=Metallomics |language=en |volume=4 |issue=7 |pages=669–678 |doi=10.1039/c2mt20025b |issn=1756-5901 |pmc=6365107 |pmid=22692182}}</ref>, and [[Sodium/proton antiporter 1|sodium/proton]] exchangers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Landau |first1=Meytal |last2=Herz |first2=Katia |last3=Padan |first3=Etana |last4=Ben-Tal |first4=Nir |date=2007-12-28 |title=Model structure of the Na+/H+ exchanger 1 (NHE1): functional and clinical implications |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=282 |issue=52 |pages=37854–37863 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M705460200  |doi-access=free|issn=0021-9258 |pmid=17981808}}</ref> His group has also developed methods for predicting the structures and motions of membrane proteins and has applied computational approaches to questions in protein evolution and drug discovery.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fleishman |first1=Sarel J. |last2=Harrington |first2=Susan |last3=Friesner |first3=Richard A. |last4=Honig |first4=Barry |last5=Ben-Tal |first5=Nir |date=November 2004 |title=An automatic method for predicting transmembrane protein structures using cryo-EM and evolutionary data |journal=Biophysical Journal |volume=87 |issue=5 |pages=3448–3459 |doi=10.1529/biophysj.104.046417 |issn=0006-3495 |pmc=1304811 |pmid=15339802 |bibcode=2004BpJ....87.3448F }}</ref>

=== ConSurf ===
Ben-Tal has led the development of ConSurf, a computational method and web server that uses evolutionary information to identify potentially functionally important regions in proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ben Chorin |first1=Adi |last2=Masrati |first2=Gal |last3=Kessel |first3=Amit |last4=Narunsky |first4=Aya |last5=Sprinzak |first5=Josef |last6=Lahav |first6=Shlomtzion |last7=Ashkenazy |first7=Haim |last8=Ben-Tal |first8=Nir |date=2020 |title=ConSurf-DB: An accessible repository for the evolutionary conservation patterns of the majority of PDB proteins |journal=Protein Science: A Publication of the Protein Society |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=258–267 |doi=10.1002/pro.3779 |issn=1469-896X |pmc=6933843 |pmid=31702846}}</ref> The methodology maps evolutionary conservation scores onto three-dimensional molecular structures, allowing conserved regions of a protein to be visualized on its surface. The original ConSurf work was published in ''[[Bioinformatics]]'' in 2003 by a team that included Ben-Tal, Fabian Glaser, Tal Pupko, Inbal Paz, Rachel E. Bell, Dalit Bechor-Shental, and Eric Martz.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Glaser |first1=Fabian |last2=Pupko |first2=Tal |last3=Paz |first3=Inbal |last4=Bell |first4=Rachel E. |last5=Bechor-Shental |first5=Dalit |last6=Martz |first6=Eric |last7=Ben-Tal |first7=Nir |date=2003-01-01 |title=ConSurf: Identification of Functional Regions in Proteins by Surface-Mapping of Phylogenetic Information |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/19.1.163 |journal=Bioinformatics |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=163–164 |doi=10.1093/bioinformatics/19.1.163 |pmid=12499312 |issn=1367-4803|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The ConSurf project has subsequently been expanded through successive versions and databases. A 2016 paper described an updated methodology for estimating and visualizing evolutionary conservation in [[macromolecules]], while later work produced ConSurf-DB, a repository containing precomputed evolutionary conservation profiles for proteins with known structures.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Ashkenazy |first1=Haim |last2=Abadi |first2=Shiran |last3=Martz |first3=Eric |last4=Chay |first4=Ofer |last5=Mayrose |first5=Itay |last6=Pupko |first6=Tal |last7=Ben-Tal |first7=Nir |date=2016-07-08 |title=ConSurf 2016: an improved methodology to estimate and visualize evolutionary conservation in macromolecules |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=44 |issue=W1 |pages=W344–350 |doi=10.1093/nar/gkw408 |issn=1362-4962 |pmc=4987940 |pmid=27166375}}</ref>

Ben-Tal has continued to contribute to the development of ConSurf. A 2023 paper described a revised version of the system for using evolutionary information to analyze macromolecules.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Yariv |first1=Barak |last2=Yariv |first2=Elon |last3=Kessel |first3=Amit |last4=Masrati |first4=Gal |last5=Chorin |first5=Adi Ben |last6=Martz |first6=Eric |last7=Mayrose |first7=Itay |last8=Pupko |first8=Tal |last9=Ben-Tal |first9=Nir |date=2023-02-21 |title=Using evolutionary data to make sense of macromolecules with a "face-lifted" ConSurf |url=https://doi.org/10.1002/pro.4582 |journal=Protein Science |volume=32 |issue=3 |article-number=e4582 |doi=10.1002/pro.4582 |pmid=36718848 |pmc=9942591 |issn=0961-8368}}</ref>

=== Protein evolution and origins of life ===
In addition to [[structural bioinformatics]], Ben-Tal has worked on [[protein evolution]] and the emergence of protein architectures and functions. His laboratory describes this research as addressing how novel protein structures and functions arise during [[molecular evolution]].<ref name=":1" />

To trace the evolutionary history of proteins, Ben-Tal, Rachel Kolodny of [[University of Haifa]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rachel's papers |url=https://cs.haifa.ac.il/~trachel/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130211927/https://cs.haifa.ac.il/~trachel/ |archive-date=2026-01-30 |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=cs.haifa.ac.il}}</ref> and coworkers searched among large representative sets of proteins for segments that are similar in sequence (and often also in structure). They presented the results as a similarity network, using a methodology that they tailor-made for this study<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nepomnyachiy |first1=Sergey |last2=Ben-Tal |first2=Nir |last3=Kolodny |first3=Rachel |date=2015 |title=CyToStruct: Augmenting the Network Visualization of Cytoscape with the Power of Molecular Viewers |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.str.2015.02.013 |journal=Structure |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=941–948 |doi=10.1016/j.str.2015.02.013 |pmid=25865247 |issn=0969-2126}}</ref>, showing that many proteins share smaller segments with each other.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nepomnyachiy |first1=Sergey |last2=Ben-Tal |first2=Nir |last3=Kolodny |first3=Rachel |date=2014-08-12 |title=Global view of the protein universe |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=111 |issue=32 |pages=11691–11696 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1403395111 |doi-access=free |pmc=4136566 |pmid=25071170 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11111691N }}</ref>

For example, they observed the same amino acid both within a short theme shared by many [[proteins]] and within a longer theme shared only by few. Next, they searched for themes that appear in different sequence and structural contexts within proteins, calling these ''bridging themes''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kolodny |first1=Rachel |last2=Nepomnyachiy |first2=Sergey |last3=Tawfik |first3=Dan S |last4=Ben-Tal |first4=Nir |date=2021-06-01 |title=Bridging Themes: Short Protein Segments Found in Different Architectures |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msab017 |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=2191–2208 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msab017 |issn=1537-1719 |pmc=8136508 |pmid=33502503}}</ref> They found many bridging themes, with an average length of about 40 residues. Interestingly, only about half of these also share a similar structure; the different environment may have induced a conformational change. Some of the bridging themes bind ligands, which attests to their functional importance. Another testimony to the evolutionary importance of these themes is the fact that some of the most ancient [[Protein superfamily|protein folds]] (e.g. [[Rossmann fold|Rossmann]], [[Walker motifs|P-loop]], and [[TIM barrel|TIM-barrel]]) were found to share them. The bridging themes may offer hints to the emergence of earliest protein families.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=Kaiyu |last2=Ben-Tal |first2=Nir |last3=Kolodny |first3=Rachel |date=2022 |title=Similar protein segments shared between domains of different evolutionary lineages |journal=Protein Science |language=en |volume=31 |issue=9 |article-number=e4407 |doi=10.1002/pro.4407 |pmid=36040261 |pmc=9387206 |issn=0961-8368}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Longo |first1=Liam M |last2=Jabłońska |first2=Jagoda |last3=Vyas |first3=Pratik |last4=Kanade |first4=Manil |last5=Kolodny |first5=Rachel |last6=Ben-Tal |first6=Nir |last7=Tawfik |first7=Dan S |date=2020-12-09 |title=On the emergence of P-Loop NTPase and Rossmann enzymes from a Beta-Alpha-Beta ancestral fragment |journal=eLife |language=en |volume=9 |article-number=e64415 |doi= 10.7554/eLife.64415|doi-access=free |pmid=33295875 |pmc=7758060 |issn=2050-084X}}</ref>

 To further understand the evolutionary emergence of protein-ligand binding, Ben-Tal and colleagues studied how proteins recognize the [[Adenine nucleotide translocator|adenine moieties]] of [[Cofactor (biochemistry)|enzyme cofactors]]. These cofactors (e.g. ATP, NAD, and FAD) have been present on Earth since the beginning of life. Ben-Tal and coworkers superimposed the structures of around 1,000 proteins based on their bound adenine-containing cofactors, and compared the patterns of hydrogen bonds that mediate adenine binding. The analysis showed that evolution has fully exploited adenine’s functional groups. In agreement with previous observations, the team found that on the protein side, these interactions were mediated by linear sequence motifs. However, additional motifs, beyond previously recorded, have been found. They found some evolutionarily distinct proteins that nevertheless shared similar adenine-binding motifs. They also found that adenine recognition often involved specific protein themes, which contained the binding motifs. The analysis offers a possible scenario for the emergence of ligand binding, where primordial peptides with minimal binding activity have gradually evolved into contemporary proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Narunsky |first1=Aya |last2=Kessel |first2=Amit |last3=Solan |first3=Ron |last4=Alva |first4=Vikram |last5=Kolodny |first5=Rachel |last6=Ben-Tal |first6=Nir |date=2020-02-20 |title=On the evolution of protein–adenine binding |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=117 |issue=9 |pages=4701–4709 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1911349117 |doi-access=free |pmid=32079721 |pmc=7060716 |bibcode=2020PNAS..117.4701N |issn=0027-8424}}</ref>

In 2025, Ben-Tal co-authored a review in ''[[Current Opinion in Structural Biology]]'' examining protein emergence and evolution.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Ezerzer |first1=Yishi |last2=Frenkel-Pinter |first2=Moran |last3=Kolodny |first3=Rachel |last4=Ben-Tal |first4=Nir |date=2025 |title=A building blocks perspective on protein emergence and evolution |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbi.2025.102996 |journal=Current Opinion in Structural Biology |volume=91 |article-number=102996 |doi=10.1016/j.sbi.2025.102996 |pmid=39919321 |issn=0959-440X|doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2026, he co-authored an AI-based research on computational representations of protein sequence and structure, and a perspective on the future of computational biology for macromolecules in the context of AI.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Guy |last2=Axel |first2=Gabriel |last3=Longo |first3=Liam M. |last4=Ben-Tal |first4=Nir |last5=Kolodny |first5=Rachel |date=2026-08-11 |title=Contrastive learning unites sequence and structure in a global representation of protein space |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=123 |issue=32 |article-number=e2532702123 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2532702123 |pmid=42546201 |pmc=13462929 |issn=0027-8424}}</ref>

=== Applied research ===
Ben-Tal has participated in research addressing biological systems of medical and security significance. His work has included computational analysis of [[membrane]] transport proteins and studies related to [[Memory|molecular mechanisms]] underlying disease and [[drug discovery]].<ref name=":4" />

In collaboration with researchers from Turkey and Israel, he co-led a NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme project on the MntABC transporter of ''[[Bacillus anthracis]]''. The project investigated the structure and functional dynamics of the transporter and sought potential compounds capable of inhibiting its activity. Ben-Tal, [[Türkan Haliloğlu]], and Oded Lewinson were the project's co-directors. The project received the 2018 NATO SPS Partnership Prize in the field of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear defence, with the award presented at NATO headquarters in November 2018.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=NATO Science Partnership Prize awarded to three outstanding projects |url=https://www.nato.int/en/news-and-events/articles/news/2019/02/12/nato-science-partnership-prize-awarded-to-three-outstanding-projects |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) |language=en}}</ref>

=== Academic service ===
Ben-Tal has served on the editorial boards of scientific journals including ''[[eLife]]'', ''[[Journal of Biological Chemistry]],'' and ''BBA Biomembranes.'' At present he is Senior Editor with ''[[Protein Science]]'' (since 2021)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Protein Science |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/1469896x/homepage/editorialboard.html |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=Wiley Online Library |language=en |doi=10.1002/(ISSN)1469-896X}}</ref>, and Associate Editor with ''[[PLoS Computational Biology]]'' (since 2013). He has also participated in scientific committees associated with international computational biology conferences, including the [[Intelligent Systems for Molecular Biology]] (ISMB) and the European Conference on Computational Biology (ECCB).<ref name=":3" />

He is a member of the Edmond J. Safra Center for Bioinformatics at [[Tel Aviv University]], where his laboratory is part of the center's research community.<ref name=":2" />

=== Books ===
Ben-Tal has also collaborated with Dr. Amit Kessel on research and teaching concerning structural biology and the origin of life. They co-authored ''Introduction to Proteins: Structure, Function, and Motion'', first published in 2010, with a second edition published in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introduction to Proteins: Structure, Function, and Motion, Second Edition |url=https://www.routledge.com/Introduction-to-Proteins-Structure-Function-and-Motion-Second-Edition/Kessel-Ben-Tal/p/book/9781498747172 |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=Routledge & CRC Press |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Ben-Tal was awarded the Abraham E. Kazan Chair of Structural Biology at [[Tel Aviv University]] in 2018.<ref name=":2" /> He was also a recipient, with collaborators, of the 2018 [[NATO Science for Peace and Security]] Programme Partnership Prize for the project on the ''Bacillus anthracis'' MntABC transporter.<ref name=":9" />
